extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American constitutional law and political history; general readers studying U.S. state constitutions
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and analyzing the provisions, tendencies, and interpretive rules found in U.S. state constitutions (Bills of Rights, miscellaneous provisions, judicial treatment, and historical development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of religious opinion and worship
rubrics_metrics.description: All provide for full freedom of religious opinion and worship, and for the equality before the law of all religious denominations and their members; many forbid the establishment of any particular church or sect, and declare that no public money ought to be applied in aid of any religious body or sectarian institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and exceptions noted: Delaware declares it the duty of all men frequently to assemble for public worship; Vermont requires that every sect ought to observe the Sabbath; thirteen States add that freedom of conscience does not excuse acts of licentiousness or practices inconsistent with the peace and safety of the State; Mississippi (1890) specified the Bible may not be excluded from schools; Idaho, Montana, Utah expressly denounce bigamy and polygamy as crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government originates with the people / purpose of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Some constitutions (e.g., Louisiana 1898) declare that 'all government, of right, originates with the people' and that its only legitimate end is to secure justice, preserve peace, and promote the interest and happiness of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a normative preface setting the aims of state governmental power and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural rights to life, liberty, and pursuit of happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: A large majority declare that 'all men have a natural, inherent, and inalienable right to enjoy and defend life and liberty,' and (except Missouri) add the 'natural right to pursue happiness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as fundamental declaratory rights in many State Bills of Rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to acquire, possess, and protect property
rubrics_metrics.description: Most declare that all men have 'a natural right to acquire, possess, and protect property.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some States (Arkansas, Kentucky historically) insisted this right is 'before and higher than any constitutional sanction.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to travel on public conveyances
rubrics_metrics.description: Some constitutions (e.g., Mississippi and Louisiana in 1868) provided that 'the right of all citizens to travel upon public conveyances shall not be infringed upon nor in any manner abridged.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noted that both States later dropped this injunction; example of specific personal-right provisions inserted in constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to alter, reform, or abolish government
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions may declare that absolute arbitrary power exists nowhere in a republic and that all men have an 'inalienable and indefeasible right to alter, reform, or abolish their government in such manner as they may deem proper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kentucky (1891) language exemplifies constitutional statement empowering popular change as a right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of writing and speaking opinions / libel evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: All constitutions in one form or another secure the freedom of writing and speaking opinions; some add that the truth of a libel may be given in evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expresses press/speech protections and procedural evidentiary rules in libel cases (jury determining law as well as fact in some states).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of public meeting and petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all secure the freedom of public meeting and petition; e.g., Florida (1886) and Kentucky (1891) explicitly provided the right to assemble, instruct representatives, and petition the legislature for redress of grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen as important rights though usually least likely to be infringed by State governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on ex post facto laws and impairment of contracts; takings compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many provide that no ex post facto law, nor law impairing the obligation of a contract, shall be passed by the State legislature; and that private property shall not be taken by the State without just compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard protections of vested rights and property against retroactive or confiscatory legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of titles of nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Many forbid the creation of any title of nobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of republican and anti-aristocratic provisions in State constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious tests and ineligibility for office in some states
rubrics_metrics.description: Some constitutions declared a person ineligible for office if he denies the existence of God or fails to believe in future rewards and punishments; in some States such persons were also incompetent as witnesses or jurors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnoted examples: Arkansas, Maryland, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Texas had such ineligibility provisions; Pennsylvania and Tennessee had belief requirements; shows variation and religious qualifications still present in some constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to bear arms with legislative regulation allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Many declare that the right of citizens to bear arms shall never be denied; some States add that the legislature shall have power to regulate the wearing of arms to prevent crime, and several allow forbidding carrying concealed weapons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tennessee (1870) allows legislature to regulate wearing of arms; Texas and eight other states allow legislature to forbid carrying concealed weapons; practical consequences for public-safety regulation noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of bringing armed men into the State to suppress domestic violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Several constitutions forbid armed men to be brought into the State 'for the suppression of domestic violence' to prevent employers from using armed forces in labor disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted at preventing private or employer use of force in industrial/labor conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estates of suicides descend in ordinary course
rubrics_metrics.description: Some constitutions declare that the estates of suicides shall descend in the ordinary course of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A particular private-law rule inserted in constitutional text in certain States.

rubrics_metrics.name: No corruption of blood or forfeiture after treason conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Most provide that conviction for treason shall not work corruption of blood nor forfeiture of estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection against hereditary punishment and excessive forfeiture for treason convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public school segregation or anti-discrimination provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Eight forbade white and colored children to be taught in the same public schools, while Wyoming provided that no distinction shall be made in public schools on account of sex, race, or colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows divergence among States: some constitutionalize segregation, others prohibit discrimination by sex/race.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury declared inviolate with permitted variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many declare the right of trial by jury to be inviolate, even while permitting the parties to waive it; several States empower juries to render verdicts by majorities and a few permit juries of less than twelve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional protection of jury trial with flexibility in verdict majorities and jury size in civil cases in some States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of imprisonment for debt except in fraud; reasonable bail
rubrics_metrics.description: Some forbid imprisonment for debt, except in case of fraud, and secure the acceptance of reasonable bail, except for the gravest charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical debtor-protection clauses and bail guarantees in State constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetuities and monopolies prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: Several declare that 'perpetuities and monopolies are contrary to the genius of a free State, and ought not to be allowed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-monopoly and anti-perpetuity policy statements embedded in constitutional text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbidding hereditary honours, privileges, or emoluments
rubrics_metrics.description: Many forbid the granting of any hereditary honours, privileges, or emoluments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinforces republican equality and avoidance of aristocratic privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: No property qualification for political rights; opposition to secret societies
rubrics_metrics.description: North Carolina declares that as 'political rights and privileges are not dependent upon or modified by property, no property qualification ought to affect the right to vote or hold office'; it also declares secret political societies dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional commitment to equal political rights regardless of property and suspicion of secret political organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral standards for public life (Massachusetts example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Massachusetts's constitution exhorts adherence to 'piety, justice, moderation, temperance, industry, and frugality' as necessary to preserve liberty and to require of law-givers an exact and constant observance of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit moral-virtue injunction placed in constitutional preface to influence civic and official conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property rights of aliens and restrictions on alien land ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Some States (South Dakota, Wyoming) provide that aliens shall have the same rights of property as citizens; Montana limits this to mining property; Washington prohibits alien ownership of land except for mining purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows State-by-State variation in constitutional treatment of aliens' property rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against malicious interference with employment
rubrics_metrics.description: North Dakota (1889) enacts that 'Every citizen shall be free to obtain employment wherever possible, and any person, corporation, or agent maliciously interfering or hindering in any way any citizen from obtaining, or enjoying employment already obtained ... shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An example of detailed labor-protective provisions inserted in a State constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation in executive offices and limits on religious gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Maryland (1867) stated that long continuance in executive power is dangerous to liberty and enacts that rotation in executive departments is one of the securities of freedom; it also pronounces gifts for religious purposes void unless sanctioned by the legislature (with limited exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional mechanisms to prevent entrenched executive power and to control religious endowments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lands for reservoirs/mining as public use subject to regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Montana and Idaho declare the use of lands for constructing reservoirs, water-courses, or ways for mining or irrigation to be a public use, subject to State regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional recognition of certain resource-utilization activities as public uses subject to regulation and potential takings rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: State may engage in occupations/business for public purposes (with limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oklahoma provides that 'the right of the State to engage in any occupation or business for public purposes shall not be denied or prohibited' but limits its agricultural enterprises to 'scientific, educational or charitable purposes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional authorization for state enterprises with enumerated limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutions often include minute miscellaneous provisions better suited to statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: State constitutions frequently contain detailed provisions of general law—administrative law, judicial procedure, banking, railways, salaries, quorum rules, appeals, venue changes, school board arrangements, and many other minute regulations—that might more properly be left to ordinary statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes the lack of a clear line between constitutional and ordinary statutory matters and gives examples (stationery procurement, storage rates for corn, bank liabilities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for constitutional minuteness: convenience, distrust of legislatures, desire for direct action
rubrics_metrics.description: Four reasons suggested for the confusion: Americans' lack of love for scientific arrangement; constitutions used as convenient opportunities to enunciate doctrines and carry reforms; distrust of legislatures leading to narrowing legislative sphere by constitution; wish of people to act directly rather than through representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanatory account of why constitutions contain so many detailed provisions; not a prescriptive rule but a diagnostic rubric for understanding constitutional content.

rubrics_metrics.name: State constitutions' reduced capacity for expansive construction
rubrics_metrics.description: State instruments have less capacity for expansion by interpretation or usage than the Federal Constitution because they are more easily amended and are far longer and more detailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: state constitutional provisions often need less judicial 'filling in' and leave less room for evolving common-law-style construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of State legislative power absent affirmative inhibition
rubrics_metrics.description: A State government is a natural growth that prima facie possesses all powers incident to any government; if a question arises whether a State legislature can pass a law, the presumption is that it can do so and positive grounds must be adduced to show it cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with Federal government (powers only those conferred); thus constitutional prohibitions on state legislative acts must be affirmatively shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial rules of interpretation — deference to legislature and harmonizing construction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a well-established rule that judges will lean in favour of the validity of a legislative Act: doubts as to constitutionality are solved in favour of the statute; where a legislature has discretion, courts assume it was wisely exercised; where a statute's construction is doubtful, adopt construction that harmonizes with the Constitution and enables it to take effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges must not inquire into motives nor refuse to apply an Act merely because obtained by fraud or because they consider it unjust; an Act is only void if shown to violate constitutional guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of statutes adjudged unconstitutional
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statute is adjudged unconstitutional it is as if it had never been: rights cannot be built under it; contracts depending on it are void; it protects no one who acted under it; no one can be punished for refusing obedience prior to decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also applies to any unconstitutional part of an Act; such parts are regarded as never having legal force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural device: advisory opinions from judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Some State constitutions provide that supreme court judges may be called upon by the governor or either house to deliver their opinions upon questions of law without waiting for cases to arise; these opinions procure judicial and non-partisan interpretation in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections: opinions given before statutes' operation lack the context of litigation and counsel; in most States such opinions are treated as advisory and not binding if the point later arises in litigation (exceptions: Maine, Colorado).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial reluctance to disturb long-acquiesced legislative practice or overturn precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest State courts may depart from previous views, but are reluctant because such changes unsettle the law; sometimes courts refuse to disturb a long-acquiesced legislative practice though they might have declared it unconstitutional when new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because State constitutions are easier to amend, courts may be more hesitant to change settled practice; illustrates a judicial policy of legal stability.
